newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich appears headed for re-election as speaker.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich appears headed for re-election as speaker.

text.p: The U.S. House of Representatives began voting for its speaker on Tuesday and appeared certain to re-elect Newt Gingrich despite a rebellion by a few Republicans over of his ethical violations.
After a meeting of House Republicans just hours before the House began to vote, it remained unclear how many Republicans would refuse to support Gingrich.
Rep Wayne Gilchrist of Maryland told reporters after the meeting, "It may be close" with "close to nine" members defecting. Five members have said publicly they will not vote for Gingrich.

Republican leaders urged potential defectors to abstain by voting "present" rather than voting for another choice which could result in failure to get a majority and require further ballots and possible further erosion of support.
Gingrich could not afford to lose many votes among Republicans. Their majority in the House over the Democrats is just 227 to 207 with one independent who usually votes with the Democrats.
House Whip Tom DeLay told reporters that a "very contrite" Gingrich apologised to his colleagues for his ethical mistakes both at Tuesday's meeting and at a meeting Monday night.
Gingrich, emerging from the meeting, said in response to shouted questions, said only "doing great."

The vote was scheduled one day before the House ethics committee begins the process of deciding what penalty to impose on Gingrich. He has admitted to bringing discredit to the House by not doing enough to prevent use of tax-exempt donations in a partisan political activity and giving false information to investigators. He has said this was unintentional.
Immediately after Gingrich was nominated as speaker, Democrats sought to delay the vote in view of what Representative Vic Fazio of California called "the extraordinary circumstances we have today."
The majority Republicans rejected the proposal, although four broke with the majority to vote with the Democrats. The vote was 222-210.

Gingrich was bidding to become the first Republican speaker to be re-elected in successive congresses for 68 years as new polls were published showing a majority of Americans believed Gingrich should be replaced.
A CNN/USA Today/Gallup poll showed that 65 per cent of those asked believed Gingrich should be replaced and 51 percent of Republicans said he should not be.
A CBS News poll showed 51 opercent of those questioned believing the charges against Gingrich were serious enough to justify his removal.
